title: Ezra 10:1–17
context: As Ezra prays and weeps before God’s house, a great assembly of men, women, and children gathers and weeps bitterly. Shecaniah confesses the community’s trespass and proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives and the children born to them, urging Ezra to act. Ezra has the leaders swear to do so, then fasts and mourns. A proclamation summons all the returned exiles to Jerusalem within three days on pain of forfeiture and exclusion. In the rain of the ninth month, Ezra charges the assembly to confess and separate themselves; the people agree but ask for an orderly process through local elders and judges. A few men stand against the plan, though the exact sense of 10:15 is uncertain. A commission examines the cases over about three months. The narrator reports these steps as the community’s response to its stated concern for covenant faithfulness; the text does not describe what provision was made for the women and children. Readers across traditions wrestle with this passage, and many read it alongside texts such as Ruth and 1 Corinthians 7:12–14, which address other circumstances.

verses.text: Now while Ezra prayed and made confession, weeping and casting himself down before God’s house, there was gathered together to him out of Israel a very great assembly of men and women and children; for the people wept very bitterly.
verses.arminianNotes: As Ezra prays and weeps before God’s house, a great assembly of men, women, and children gathers and weeps bitterly. Arminian readers note that the whole community, including families, is moved by Ezra’s grief and prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God working through Ezra’s confession to stir the people’s hearts. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a moment of communal sorrow, and they note that women and children are present in the assembly.

verses.text: Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered Ezra, “We have trespassed against our God, and have married foreign women of the peoples of the land. Yet now there is hope for Israel concerning this thing.
verses.arminianNotes: Shecaniah confesses that they have trespassed by marrying foreign women, yet says there is hope for Israel. Arminian readers note that he speaks as one of the people, and that his family is later named in the list (10:26, the sons of Elam).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the word of hope a confidence in God’s mercy even after grave sin. Both traditions read the verse as the turning point from grief to action, with hope grounded in God’s willingness to forgive.

verses.text: Now therefore let’s make a covenant with our God to put away all the wives and those who are born of them, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God. Let it be done according to the law.
verses.arminianNotes: Shecaniah proposes a covenant to put away the wives and the children born to them, according to the law. Arminian readers report the proposal as the narrator gives it, and note that the text does not describe what provision was made for the women and children.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “according to the law” likely points to passages such as Deuteronomy 7:3, though no law prescribes this exact step. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, without endorsement or polemic, and acknowledge its difficulty.

verses.text: Arise, for the matter belongs to you and we are with you. Be courageous, and do it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Shecaniah urges Ezra to arise, for the matter belongs to him and the people are with him. Arminian readers note that the community offers its support, making the decision a shared one rather than imposed by Ezra alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call to courage as recalling words spoken to leaders such as Joshua. Both traditions read the verse as the people’s encouragement to Ezra, reported as part of the narrative without further evaluation.

verses.text: Then Ezra arose, and made the chiefs of the priests, the Levites, and all Israel to swear that they would do according to this word. So they swore.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra has the chief priests, Levites, and all Israel swear to do according to this word. Arminian readers note that the oath binds the leaders publicly, so that the community commits itself together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath as a formal covenant act before God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recording the leaders’ commitment, without assessing every aspect of the course they chose.

verses.text: Then Ezra rose up from before God’s house, and went into the room of Jehohanan the son of Eliashib. When he came there, he didn’t eat bread or drink water, for he mourned because of the trespass of the exiles.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra goes to the room of Jehohanan son of Eliashib and fasts, mourning the exiles’ trespass. Arminian readers note Ezra’s continued grief, showing that his concern is not merely procedural but deeply personal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the identity of this Jehohanan and his relation to other men of that name (compare Nehemiah 12:22–23) is debated. Both traditions read the verse as showing Ezra’s mourning, without resolving questions of chronology.

verses.text: They made a proclamation throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the children of the captivity, that they should gather themselves together to Jerusalem;
verses.arminianNotes: A proclamation goes throughout Judah and Jerusalem for all the returned exiles to gather at Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the public and inclusive summons, calling the whole community to address the matter together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly as a covenant gathering of God’s people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the beginning of a formal process that will involve the entire returned community.

verses.text: and that whoever didn’t come within three days, according to the counsel of the princes and the elders, all his possessions should be forfeited, and he himself separated from the assembly of the captivity.
verses.arminianNotes: Anyone who does not come within three days will forfeit his possessions and be separated from the assembly. Arminian readers note the seriousness of the penalty, which shows how weighty the leaders considered the matter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the penalty as reflecting the authority of the community’s leaders over its members. Both traditions report the measure as the text gives it, and read it within its historical setting.

verses.text: Then all the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered themselves together to Jerusalem within the three days. It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month; and all the people sat in the wide place in front of God’s house, trembling because of this matter, and because of the great rain.
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Judah and Benjamin gather on the twentieth day of the ninth month, trembling because of the matter and the heavy rain. Arminian readers note the vivid detail of people sitting in the open square during the rainy season.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trembling as reflecting both the gravity of the issue and the discomfort of the weather. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical narrative, setting the scene for Ezra’s address.

verses.text: Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, “You have trespassed, and have married foreign women, increasing the guilt of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra tells the assembly they have trespassed by marrying foreign women, increasing Israel’s guilt. Arminian readers note that Ezra names the issue plainly, holding the community responsible for its choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Ezra’s words as applying the law to the community’s situation. Both traditions read the charge as concerning covenant faithfulness, as stated in 9:1–2 and 9:11–12, and avoid extending it beyond that setting.

verses.text: Now therefore make confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers and do his pleasure. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign women.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra calls them to confess to the LORD, do his pleasure, and separate from the peoples of the land and the foreign women. Arminian readers note that confession and obedience are joined together in the call to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the command as Ezra’s application of covenant separation in this specific crisis. Shared ground: both traditions report the verse as the narrator gives it, while acknowledging that readers find the measure difficult.

verses.text: Then all the assembly answered with a loud voice, “We must do as you have said concerning us.
verses.arminianNotes: The assembly answers with a loud voice that they must do as Ezra has said. Arminian readers note the people’s willing agreement, showing that they accept the charge laid before them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the response as a sign of the community’s acknowledgment of guilt. Both traditions read the verse as the people’s consent, recorded without comment on the moral complexity of what follows.

verses.text: But the people are many, and it is a time of much rain, and we are not able to stand outside. This is not a work of one day or two, for we have greatly transgressed in this matter.
verses.arminianNotes: The people say they are many, it is rainy, and the matter cannot be done in a day or two. Arminian readers note the practical wisdom of the people, who recognize that a careful process will take time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as seeking an orderly and fair handling of each case. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reasonable appeal, which leads to a more deliberate procedure.

verses.text: Now let our princes be appointed for all the assembly, and let all those who are in our cities who have married foreign women come at appointed times, and with them the elders of every city and its judges, until the fierce wrath of our God is turned from us, until this matter is resolved.”
verses.arminianNotes: They ask that leaders be appointed and that each case come with local elders and judges, until God’s wrath is turned away. Arminian readers note the concern for due process, with cases heard in the presence of local leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hope of turning away God’s anger as the motive behind the community’s actions. Both traditions read the verse as describing a structured process, and neither assumes how each case was decided.

verses.text: Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahzeiah the son of Tikvah stood up against this; and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah stand against this, helped by Meshullam and Shabbethai. Arminian readers note that the meaning is uncertain: they may have opposed the plan or opposed the delay.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some read the phrase as supervising rather than opposing, so the verse is hedged. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge the uncertainty and avoid building conclusions on this verse.

verses.text: The children of the captivity did so. Ezra the priest, with certain heads of fathers’ households, after their fathers’ houses, and all of them by their names, were set apart; and they sat down in the first day of the tenth month to examine the matter.
verses.arminianNotes: The exiles do so, and Ezra with heads of families sits on the first day of the tenth month to examine the matter. Arminian readers note that the process involves careful examination rather than a hasty decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appointed leaders acting with authority on behalf of the community. Both traditions read the verse as describing the commission’s work, reported without detail on how individual cases were judged.

verses.text: They finished with all the men who had married foreign women by the first day of the first month.
verses.arminianNotes: The commission finishes with all the men who had married foreign women by the first day of the first month. Arminian readers note that the work took about three months, suggesting case-by-case attention.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completion as the end of the community’s formal response. Shared ground: the verse reports the conclusion of the process, and both traditions note that the text gives no further details of outcomes.
